name: Coatlán-Loxicha Zapotec, CLZ, San Baltazar Loxicha
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary Grace. 2004. A Coatlán-Loxicha Zapotec Grammar (Mexico). PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. Author-posted open PDF,https://rosemarybeamdeazcona.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/zapotec_beam2004_s.pdf(618 pp.).
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonetics and Phonology, sec. 2.2.3 'Stress', pp. 81-82 for the rule; section runs pp. 81-88, 2.2.4 'Intonation' begins p. 89. p. 98 prints page number 81 and the heading '2.2.3 Stress'; p. 99 prints 82 with 'The change from a high to a non-high tone..' and 'In sum..'. Exceptions spans: p. 81 (onomatopoeia), p. 84 (unreduced vs reduced compounds), p. 86 (compounds with high-toned stressed ultimas). Identity: p. 7 (Ethnologue ZPS/ZPX split rejected), p. 363 (primary consultant from San Baltazar Loxicha).
catalog_quote: Due to historical non-tonic vowel deletion, most CLZ words are monosyllabic. When considering lexical stress, the lone syllable of a monosyllabic root must be the stressed syllable, although certainly a given word may lack stress syntactically, a topic I touch on in 2.2.4. Lexical stress is only an issue in CLZ when there are polysyllabic words. There are only three types of words with more than one syllable in CLZ: onomatopoeia, compounds and loanwords. ... Polysyllabic words in CLZ have final stress. Final syllables tend to be heavy CVC syllables although they may be light CV syllables. Pre-tonic syllables tend to be light (C)V syllables although they may be heavy (C)VC syllables. Unstressed syllables can only take high tone while stressed syllables can take any tone, although high tone is the least common of the five tones in stressed syllables. ... In sum, an unstressed syllable is any non-final syllable with high tone. All final syllables are stressed and the prominence which is stress can be attained either by a non-high tone or by syllable weight or both.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary Grace. 2004. A Coatlán-Loxicha Zapotec Grammar (Mexico). PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley.
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2 Phonetics and Phonology, sec. 2.2.3 'Stress', p.81 and p.82 (pp.98-99)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File checked: (+, extracted text), Beam de Azcona 2004 Berkeley dissertation, author-posted open copy (rosemarybeamdeazcona.com), 618 pp; present and accurate. Locator verified: extracted text of p.98 shows printed p.81 with heading '2.2.3 Stress'; section runs pp.81-88 (the text), 2.2.4 Intonation begins p.89. Every quoted span is present verbatim at the stated pages: p.81 'Due to historical non-tonic vowel deletion, most CLZ words are monosyllabic. When considering lexical stress, the lone syllable of a monosyllabic root must be the stressed syllable, although certainly a given word may lack stress syntactically..'; 'There are only three types of words with more than one syllable in CLZ:…
new_statements.rule_in_words: CLZ is tonal and mostly monosyllabic; in the polysyllabic words that exist (reduced compounds, Spanish loans, opaque old compounds) stress is on the final syllable. Pre-tonic syllables are light and carry only high tone (arguably toneless); the tonic final syllable carries the full five-way tone contrast and is usually heavy; in all-high-toned loans the final syllable shows higher pitch and amplitude (Fig. 21). No consistent durational correlate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described as such; unreduced compounds are said to have stress on both roots, reduced compounds only on the final root (p.84).
new_statements.exceptions: Onomatopoeia excluded as outside normal phonology; unreduced compounds/lexical phrases stressed on each root; loanword tone on the stressed syllable (high vs rising) is not fully predictable, but stress placement stays final because post-tonic Spanish vowels are deleted (pp.86-88); a word 'may lack stress syntactically' (p.81, cf. 2.2.4 intonation).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical/word stress, stated for CLZ as a whole with San Baltazar Loxicha as the primary dialect of record; examples are isolation/elicitation forms (audio on the diss. CD); phrase-level destressing and declination treated separately in 2.2.4.
new_statements.identity_note: Beam de Azcona (2004:7) describes 'Coatlán-Loxicha Zapotec' (CLZ) as one language that Ethnologue splits into [ZPS] Coatlán Zapotec (Glottolog coat1243) and [ZPX] 'San Baltázar Loxicha Zapoteco / Northwestern Pochutla' (sanb1241); she treats them as mutually intelligible dialects. Her primary consultant is Lázaro Díaz Pacheco of San Baltazar Loxicha (p.363), the tone figures (Figs. 10, 20) are explicitly SBL, and dialect differences (SBL vs Santa María Coatlán, San Miguel Coatlán) are footnoted where relevant; the stress section 2.2.3 is stated for CLZ as a whole with SBL forms. The same PDF is also held under for the Coatlán code.

tone_statements.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2019. Southern Zapotec verb classes. Amerindia 41: 121-165. DOI 10.56551/nvjz1964.
tone_statements.quote: Coatec Zapotec examples in this paper are presented in a practical orthography. In this orthography, the symbol <’> indicates a glottalized vowel. Tones are indicated with diacritics: high tone á, low tone à, falling tone â, rising tone ǎ. Tone is neutralized on glottalized vowels. … The habitual form (as long as it occurs without a first person subject) has the tone that is the underlying lexical tone of the verb root. … The underlying low tone can remain, as in ‘massage’, it can change to glottal tone in the completive as in ‘explode’ or falling tone as in ‘holler’.
tone_statements.summary: Four tones (high, low, falling, rising), neutralized on glottalized vowels; verb roots carry lexical tone; aspect/mood and 1sg marked by tone changes (low>rising, falling>high, low>glottal/falling).

tone_statements.quote: Esta lengua tiene: • Prominencia en la última sílaba de compuestos, contrastes tonales en la sílaba tónica y en los enclíticos únicamente • 5 categorías tonales contrastivas: alto, bajo, descendente, ascendente, glotal • Duración y rasgos laríngeos asociados a categorías tonales • Tono contrastivo en enclíticos: alto, descendente • Morfología tonal que se puede explicar con un tono alto flotante • Sandhi tonal provocado por el tono ascendente • Upstep … ‘cangrejo’ /mbé/ [mbe ˦] • ‘neblina’ /mbè/ [mbeːˀ ˨] • ‘araña’ /mbê/ [mbeˑ ˦˩] • ‘tortuga’ /mbě/ [mbeːˀ˨˥ • ‘luna’ /mbeʔ/ [mbeʔ]
tone_statements.translation: This language has: prominence on the last syllable of compounds, tonal contrasts on the tonic syllable and on enclitics only; 5 contrastive tonal categories: high, low, falling, rising, glottal; duration and laryngeal features associated with tonal categories; contrastive tone on enclitics: high, falling; tonal morphology explainable by a floating high tone; tone sandhi triggered by the rising tone; upstep … 'crab' /mbé/ [mbe 4], 'fog' /mbè/ [mbe:ˀ 2], 'spider' /mbê/ [mbe 41], 'turtle' /mbě/ [mbe:ˀ 25], 'moon' /mbeʔ/ [mbeʔ]

tone_statements.summary: Five contrastive tones (high, low, falling, rising, glottal) on the tonic final syllable only; enclitics contrast high vs falling; floating high marks 1sg/potential; rising tone causes sandhi, upstep.

tone_statements.translation: in Coatec the tonal contrasts have been neutralized in glottalized syllables. … For this reason glottalization has become tone, i.e. it is now a category that contrasts with the other tones of the language. … Table 5. Examples of the tones of Coatec (San Baltazar Loxicha variety): high, low, falling, rising, glottal: mbé 'crab', mbè 'fog', mbê 'spider', mbě 'turtle', mbeʔ 'moon; butterfly' … Table 6. The tones of Coatec Zapotec: High, Low, Rising, Falling, Glottal.

tone_statements.summary: Five contrastive tones in San Baltazar Loxicha Coatec: high, low, falling, rising, glottal (tone neutralized on glottalized syllables); floating high marks potential/1sg; no tone contrast off stress.

tone_statements.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 1998. Preliminary remarks on tone in Coatlán-Loxicha Zapotec. Santa Barbara Papers in Linguistics 8 (Proceedings from the First Workshop on American Indigenous Languages), 3-14. Santa Barbara: UCSB Department of Linguistics.
tone_statements.quote: 1. There are four tones in the San Baltazar Loxicha variety of CLZ. These contrast with glottalized syllables which do not bear contrastive pitch patterns: … The high tone moves somewhat more than the low tone but not as much as true contour tones. … The falling tone typically starts in the range of200-180Hz., though sometimes lower, and falls 50Hz. or more. The rising tone usually starts around 120 or 130Hz. and rises to anywhere from 170Hz. to over 200Hz. … Glottalization does contrast with the four other tones. … Here I will treat phonemic glottalization as a separate category from tone.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 3-4, secs. 1-1.1 (example (1) mbé 'cangrejo' H, mbè 'neblina' L, mbê 'araña' F, mbě 'tortuga' R, mbe7 'luna' glottalized)
tone_statements.summary: Four tones (high, low, falling, rising) on mostly monosyllabic words; glottalized syllables contrast with all four but carry no contrastive pitch; tone sandhi from a floating high (potential, 1sg).

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.3 'Stress' pp.81-88: most words monosyllabic (historical non-tonic vowel deletion); polysyllabic words (compounds, loans) have final stress; unstressed = non-final high-toned (arguably toneless) syllable; prominence via non-high tone and/or heavy final syllable, plus higher pitch/amplitude in all-high loans (Fig. 21 éskópét); no consistent length correlate; reduced compounds final stress, unreduced compounds stress on both roots; recent Spanish loans delete post-tonic vowels so stress ends up final; words may lack stress syntactically (2.2.4).

sources.citation: Beam de Azcona, Rosemary G. 2023. The tonal morphology of the potential in Coatec Zapotec (Di'zhke'): implications for early Zapotecan tone, *ʔ, and verb classes. Journal of Historical Linguistics (author preprint).
sources.note: Historical: since Proto-Trochaic-Zapotec the root-initial syllable is the tonic (stressed, per Hyman 2006) syllable; Coatec lost post-tonic vowels; cites Beam de Azcona in prep. 'Zapotecan Stress and its Interaction with Phonological Contrasts'. No new synchronic CLZ stress rule beyond the 2004 grammar.
